## Introduction

The atomic bombings of Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (August 9, 1945) represent one of the most consequential and debated decisions in modern history. ### Allied Leadership Perspective
President Harry Truman and his advisors faced what they perceived as a dire situation in mid-1945:
- Intelligence estimates suggested an invasion of Japan (Operation Downfall) could result in hundreds of thousands of Allied casualties
- Japan had shown fierce resistance throughout the Pacific campaign
- The war had already claimed millions of lives across multiple theaters
- There was pressure to end the conflict quickly to prevent Soviet expansion in Asia

### Japanese Leadership Perspective
Japan's leadership was deeply divided:
- Some military leaders advocated continued resistance despite devastating conventional bombing campaigns
- Emperor Hirohito and some civilian officials privately sought ways to end the war while preserving national honor
- The concept of "honorable death" (gyokusai) influenced military thinking
- Communication between factions was limited, complicating surrender negotiations

- Descriptions of unprecedented destruction and human suffering
- Long-term health effects including radiation sickness, cancer, and genetic impacts
- Social stigma faced by survivors in post-war Japan
- Calls for nuclear disarmament and peace education

### International Reactions
- Some Allied leaders expressed shock at the weapons' destructive power
- Scientists involved in the Manhattan Project had mixed reactions—some felt vindicated, others deeply troubled
- The Soviet Union accelerated its own nuclear program
- Global awareness of nuclear weapons' implications began to emerge

- Portrayed the decision as necessary to end the war
